column1: # Where each gloss in lex-ang.tsv was read.
# lemma | pos | tgt | sources | quote | stands
# The gloss is the English word an Old English word is woven for, and the
# tooltip and the word page print it back: it is the claim every reader meets
# first. Every other claim the pack makes about a word names its entry —
# etymons in ang-etymons.tsv, genders in ang-genders.tsv, phrases in
# ang-phrases.tsv — and the gloss named none until 2026-10-07, as the Latin
# Every row is read, all 356, on 2026-10-07: the 178 nouns, 81 verbs, 57
# adjectives, 22 adverbs, 13 numerals and 5 interjections. Each was read
# Wiktionary's Old English entry, from its raw text, and against
# Bosworth–Toller wherever ang-genders.tsv read a noun's gender there and
# ang-phrases.tsv a phrase's text. A script
# drafted a quote for each row from the entry's definition lines, links and
# labels read as the page prints them, and every quote was read against its
# entry; where a page holds more than one word of a spelling — hund, a dog
# and a hundred; lagu, the sea and the law — the quote is from the
# etymology that is this word, as the genders were.
# Each line names the entries it was read in, separated by spaces, the one
#                      (the title drops macrons and the dots of ċ and ġ)
# A noun cites the entry its gender was read in, so the two ledgers cannot
# read different words. Wiktionary files most Old English words under their
# þ spelling, and its page for brōðor, mūð or dēað says only "Alternative
# form of" the þ one; so does its page for meoluc, wall, hæt, wolcen and
# wicu, of meolc, weall, hætt, wolcn and wice, and so does its page for the
# adjectives sceort, nīwe, sōfte, ǣmettiġ, ēaþe and bald, and the numerals
# þrēo and siex, of scort, nīewe, sēfte, æmtiġ, īeþe, beald, þrī and six —
# the Old English six, which only looks like the English word, and the
# adverb wēnunga, of wēninga. Those twenty-one lines quote the entry named
# and cite the word's own beside it, and FORM_OF in the test lists them. þorp is quoted from Wiktionary, "village", because
# Bosworth–Toller's head, where its gender was read, gives no one English
# word: "the idea at first connected with the words is that of an
# assemblage", then of workers on an estate, and of the estate.
# Blank where the quote holds the row's English word. Otherwise it names the
# word of the quote that stands for it, because the English word is not in the
# entry. Twenty rows need one. Four are adverbs: ǣfre for "always" is
# "ever", sōna for "soon" "immediately", whose note says so, wēnunga for
# "perhaps" "possibly, perchance, maybe", and tō morgen for "tomorrow"
# "to-morrow", the dictionary's spelling of the word, as Latin crās's line
# in la-glosses.tsv names it. Six are nouns: hund for "hound" is "dog",
# setl for "chair" "seat, bench, throne", mentel for "coat" "mantle (kind of
# cloak)", rīċe for "country" "kingdom, empire", fyrhtu for "fear" "fright",
# and hūsbonda for "husband" "master of the house". Seven are verbs:
# ondrǣdan "to be scared", losian "to be lost", wēpan "to weep", weardian "to
# guard", settan "to set, establish, place", wealcan "to move around" and
# winnan "to struggle". Three are phrases, read in the Bosworth–Toller entry
# ang-phrases.tsv names, which has no English for them: wes hāl for "hello"
# is hál "often used in salutation"; for "goodbye" it is "Wesaþ hále
# valete", whose stand-in is the Latin, valete, farewell, because the
# dictionary glosses the phrase in nothing else; and iċ bidde for "please"
# is biddan "To ask, pray", as "pray" was English for please.
# Three of those rows are woven for a sense their word gained after Old
# English, and their notes say so: hūsbonda for "husband", "the householder,
# not yet the spouse"; wealcan for "walk", "it meant to roll or toss"; and
# winnan for "win", "meant to struggle or toil". Their stand-ins are the
# loosest in the ledger, and whether to weave them at all is a call written
# One row had no gloss in either dictionary. ċildclāð, woven for "baby"
# until 2026-10-07, is Wiktionary's cildclāþ, "swaddling cloth; (in the
# plural), swaddling clothes", and Bosworth–Toller's "a child-cloth, a
# swaddling-cloth" (bt:6142); its Supplement, where the gender was read, has
# no English at all. Reading this ledger found it, and it was withdrawn the
# same night: "baby" is ċild now, which Wiktionary gives as "child" and
# "baby" and Bosworth–Toller as "a child, infant" (bt:6138). QUEUED in the
# test is for a row like it: one whose line quotes what its entry does say,
# named there until the row is taught differently. It named a second the
# same night: lāh, woven for "low", is no adjective in either dictionary —
# Wiktionary's lah is only a past tense of lēon, to lend, and
# Bosworth–Toller's lah (bt:21055) a noun, "Law" — and English Wiktionary
# derives low from Middle English lah, from Old Norse lágr. "low" is hēan
# now, Wiktionary's "low, mean, abject, humble", whose source is
# Proto-Germanic *hauniz and not hēah's, high; lāh's card is the sixth
# WITHDRAWN keeps. And it named tōmorgen, tomorrow, which has no entry under
# that spelling in either dictionary: Wiktionary's tomorgen redirects to a
# Middle English page, and Bosworth–Toller writes it as two words. Its
# morgen (bt:23129) has a second sense below the first, "the morning of the
# next day, morrow", quoting "Gá and cum tó morgenne go, and come to-morrow"
# from the Pastoral Care and "Tó morgen cras" from Exodus and the Gospels;
# the first reading of the entry stopped above it. So the pack teaches tō
# morgen, a phrase ang-phrases.tsv holds, its card renamed rather than
# withdrawn because its letters are the same, and QUEUED is empty again.
# tests/tools/ang-glosses.test.ts requires every row of a part of speech it
# holds to have a line here, every line to cite Bosworth–Toller or the word's
# own Wiktionary entry, every quote to hold its English word or name the word
# standing for it, no quote to carry wikitext, every noun to cite the entry
# its gender was read in, and every phrase an entry its text was read in. It cannot tell a quote somebody copied from
# the entry from one somebody typed, nor an entry somebody read from one
